sentences.text: Sliding doors open for anything that steps in front of them.
They never ask whether you are alive.
It is seven past three in the dead of night.
You are shelving tins in aisle 5 when the front doors slide open by themselves.
The figure in the doorway is a regular, here every night at three.
A paper and a black coffee.
Tonight he only stands and stares.
The doors keep trying to shut on him, then give up and open again.
Rhea, the night manager, rams him back out with a shopping cart and turns the lock.
He bumps the glass, steps back, and bumps it again.
Up in the office, twelve security cameras watch the town.
On every single screen, someone is running.
Rhea snatches her car keys.
Her children are on the other side of town.
Forty-five minutes, she tells you.
Lock up behind me.
It is the last human voice you will hear for twelve days.
From here on, it is only you.
25,000 products, and a whole front wall made of glass.
Problem one: the glass.
There is a steel roller shutter.
It runs on mains power.
The store never closes, so it only drops once a year, on New Year's Day.
If the power fails first, you wind it down by hand, one turn at a time, with a crowd watching.
So you wind it down.
It takes 35 seconds, and it roars like a freight train.
House rule.
Nobody comes in.
Then you go back to your nightly routine.
You count stock.
Aisle 5.
7,300 tins.
Eat five a day.
That is four years of dinners from one aisle.
This building holds enough food for a lifetime.
Surviving until day 28 will be the real challenge, because food is not the problem.
Then, at 5:23, the power goes out.
The freezers fall silent.
And from the back of the store comes a heavy clunk.
The fire exit is held closed by a magnet.
And magnets need power.
You sprint the full length of the store.
